newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich's Fed blast seen reflecting tax dilemma.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich's Fed blast seen reflecting tax dilemma.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich's scolding of the Federal Reserve for raising interest rates highlighted his own predicament of wanting to cut taxes while reducing the deficit, analysts said Friday.
Stronger economic growth would help efforts to reduce the budget deficit and provide lawmakers more room to cut taxes.
The Republican leader, in his home state of Georgia, said: "It is unconscionable to have the Federal Reserve system close off economic growth because of some theoretical model."

Gingrich spoke to Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan by telephone after telling business leaders in his electoral district that he would ask the Fed chief to submit a list of policy changes that would make a 4 to 5 percent growth rate acceptable to the central bank.
The Fed had no comment on Gingrich's remarks.
Members of Congress from both sides of the aisle have criticized the Fed for its action last week when it raised interest rates for the first time in more than two years.

"One can be assured of this, just like the sun comes up in the East every day, when the Federal Reserve raises interest rates to cool down the economy there will be lots of outrage in Congress, it's a predictable result," William Beach, a senior fellow at the Heritage Foundation, said.
Beach said Gingrich's remarks were only significant if they arose from some undercurrent.

"If they were made just to complain about the Federal Reserve's actions then that's not remarkable," he said. "I think there may be something here that's related to balancing the budget, or making CPI changes, or both," Beach said, referring to the consumer price index.
Some lawmakers and analysts have said it would be nearly impossible for Congress to enact tax cuts this year while trying to balance the budget unless the CPI is lowered.

An advisory commission last December said the CPI overstated cost-of-living by 1.1 percentage points a year. Since increases in some federal benefits such as Social Security are tied to the CPI, lowering that inflation index would save the government money.
If the CPI were lowered, it would diminish reasons for the Fed to raise interest rates again, so "this may be part of the game to encourage the CPI change," Beach said.
Another analyst saw Gingrich's criticism of the Fed as an attempt at diversion from the lack of substantive activity in the House.

"Gingrich is trying to find something that he can use to get out from under his troubles," Martin Mayer, guest scholar at The Brookings Institution, said. "Congress has done nothing and not only has it done nothing, it has nothing on its schedule, so Gingrich is trying to hide that," he added.

Speaking only weeks after he was widely criticized in his own party for suggesting that Congress might have to make tax cuts a secondary priority, Gingrich called Friday for getting rid of taxes on savings and investments to boost growth.

"You want Chinese or Hong Kong or Taiwanese growth rates? You've got to have a tax system that favors economic growth. If you want more jobs and you want more wealth and you want a better future ... there should be no taxes on savings and investments," he said.
